idiom_name: libxml2 logical page behind unique_ptr owners + libxslt transform per channel
implementation_notes: Stage one builds the logical page as a libxml2 document whose pointers are adopted immediately by std::unique_ptr with the matching deleter (xmlFreeDoc, xsltFreeStylesheet), so the intermediate cannot leak on an early return or an exception; the tree stays strictly channel-neutral. Stage two compiles one stylesheet per channel once and runs xsltApplyStylesheet per render, which keeps HTML, text and XSL-FO outputs derived from the same page. Modern C++ adds nothing to the split itself - it only makes ownership exception-safe and hides the xmlChar* ceremony behind std::string_view wrappers. Choose it when XSLT stylesheets are the team's rendering technology; otherwise the sibling variant avoids the dependency entirely.
pitfalls: A raw pointer created before the wrapper that owns it is constructed leaks if anything in between throws; adopt each allocation immediately.
libxslt and libxml2 keep process-global parser flags and cleanup routines, so they are not tied to your objects and mixing a vendored and a system copy is a link-time trap.
The result document returned by xsltApplyStylesheet is owned by the caller and is not freed by xsltFreeStylesheet; forgetting xmlFreeDoc leaks one page per request.

variants.name: Hand-rolled node tree + one writer per channel
variants.idiom_name: Node{tag, attrs, children} page tree + render_html/render_text writer functions
variants.implementation_notes: When libxml2/libxslt cannot be taken (embedded targets, dependency policy), model the logical page as a tiny node struct - tag, attributes, children - and write one renderer per channel as a tree walk, for example render_html and render_text over the same Node. The split survives because the tree is channel-neutral and only the writers know about markup; what you give up is the declarative stylesheet, so escaping, vocabulary and tree lifetime become your code and a house-style change needs a recompile. Choose it for small, stable page vocabularies where the XSLT toolchain would be the larger dependency.
pitfalls: Each writer must escape for its own channel; escaping while building the tree double-escapes, and skipping it in one writer is an injection hole.
Owning the tree means owning copies and recursion depth: a deep page copied node by node costs more than a libxml2 node pool, and a recursive writer can overflow the stack on adversarial input.
Without a stylesheet the renderers are C++ code, so a look-and-feel change is a rebuild and a release - the flexibility the split is supposed to buy is reduced.
